items.title: Cross-subject decoding of imagined speech from scalp EEG: a leakage-controlled evaluation on three public corpora
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Blessing Isoyiza Adeika, Onyema Osuagwu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objective. A decoder of imagined speech that works for a new user without calibration would make a non-invasive speech interface practical. We tested whether imagined-speech content recorded with scalp electroencephalography (EEG) transfers across people, and examined why accuracy within a single person remains low. Approach. We analyzed three public corpora, ds003626, KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion and reports exact binomial thresholds, group tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. We trained decoders on each participant and tested them on every other, compared representational geometry across participants without a classifier, applied subject-level alignment, and tested five explanations for the within-subject ceiling. Main results. Across 482 ordered pairs of participants, no pair survived correction for multiple comparisons; mean pair-transfer accuracy lay within 0.006 of chance on every corpus, while every within-subject reference lay above it. Imagery against pre-stimulus rest generalized at about 0.61 after artifact and elapsed-time controls, but its decoder labelled the interval preceding imagery as imagery as often as imagery itself, so the contrast reflects a post-stimulus state, not imagery. Within subject, only the competition corpus decoded above threshold for every participant (0.3147; chance 0.200); syllable count explained little of this, but its frequency profile failed an artifact audit. Significance. In these corpora, imagined-speech content did not transfer between people through any representation we examined. Trial count per class was the only variable that ordered the corpora, which favors larger single-condition datasets over further model development.

items.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Dongyu Gong
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21176v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

items.title: Mutual Information in High-Dimensional Neural Coding
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zimo Li, Yuchang Tian, Matthew P. Leighton, Christopher W. Lynn
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating mutual information in large neural populations is limited by the exponential growth of possible neural response patterns. Here we apply a Monte Carlo framework to make this problem tractable by sampling from a conditionally independent population model fit from single-neuron responses. The estimator accurately recovers analytical ground truth, corrects finite-data bias, and scales to empirical recordings containing 100 to 10,000 neurons from visual cortex, hippocampus, and retina. Across systems, stimulus uncertainty decays exponentially with population size, revealing a simple scaling law for high-dimensional neural codes.

items.title: Contextual Probability and Operational Minimality in Tug-of-War Decision Making
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Song-Ju Kim
items.summary: arXiv:2601.10034v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What connects minimal decision-making to contextual probability? We address this question through the Tug-of-War (TOW) principle, a resource-coupled mechanism for multi-armed bandit decision-making. Starting from classical probability, we show that when reward-learning functionality and specified information requirements are fixed, minimizing the necessary relaxation of common event semantics can lead to nonclassical probability. We derive the exact minimum semantic repair and identify the conditions under which information efficiency, calibration, and compositional consistency select contextual statistics. We then construct a single quantum Tug-of-War (QTOW) instrument in which the same decision--reward process both improves stationary decision performance and drives the unconditional learned state beyond the Klyachko--Can--Binicio\u{g}lu--Shumovsky (KCBS) noncontextuality bound. A finite diagnostic based on the instrument's recovery operations also yields a corrected contextuality witness. These results connect minimal decision-making, operational economy, and the emergence of contextual probability.

items.title: FlatClip: Reusing Image Foundation Models for fMRI Representation Learning via Cortical Flatmaps
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Mo Wang, Wenhao Ye, Zihan Ning, Jiayu Zuo, Junfeng Xia, Hongkai Wen, Quanying Liu
items.summary: arXiv:2609.31204v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can the spatial organization of cortical activity help transfer frozen image representations to fMRI prediction? We introduce FlatClip, which renders cortical activity as anatomy-linked flatmaps and extracts features with a frozen SigLIP2 encoder. Only a lightweight downstream probe is trained, without fMRI-specific encoder pretraining or fine-tuning. Across four resting-state benchmarks, FlatClip outperforms the evaluated ROI-level baselines on HCP and ADNI, but is weaker on PPMI and below the strongest voxel-level models overall. On NSD visual-fMRI decoding, restricting inputs to visual or NSD-provided task-active cortex improves recognition over whole-cortex inputs. Spatial perturbations reduce performance with both retrained and fixed readouts, and anatomy-linked arrangements outperform cortical-pixel permutations across three colormaps. Together, these results demonstrate a practical route for reusing image-pretrained features in fMRI and highlight cortical arrangement and input-region selection as important design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/OneMore1/FlatClip.

items.title: Awakening as a Trait-Level Transformation of Consciousness
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Riku Ihalainen, Victor Oswald, Gulshan Kumar, Genevieve Major, Balachundhar Subramaniam, Steven Laureys, Prejaas K. B. Tewarie
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Awakening is reported across contemplative traditions yet remains poorly defined in science, where it is often conflated with transient states induced by meditation or psychedelics, obscuring its significance for theories of consciousness and cognitive architecture. We treat awakening as a functional construct capturing convergence across Hindu and Buddhist sources, phenomenological and psychometric findings, and neuroimaging evidence. Synthesizing these literatures, we find convergent evidence for reorganization across dimensions including self-related processing, affective reactivity, and temporal structure, while exposing limits of paradigms for detecting trait-level change. We argue that awakening is best understood not as a transient state but as a trait-level reorganization of experience, centered on a reduction in identification with mental contents rather than the acquisition of new content. To account for this contentless transformation, we propose the enactive-dereification model (EDM), which treats training and awakening as graded differences along a dereification gradient, from a reified to a relational mode of experience. We offer an operational definition that distinguishes awakening from state-dependent experiences and psychopathology, emphasizing dynamical flexibility and stabilization of a dereified mode. The framework yields falsifiable predictions linking independently assessed trait transformation to large-scale neural dynamics and provides a basis for distinguishing adaptive contemplative change from pathological ego-dissolution.

items.title: Statistical Mechanics of Spike Trains: Self-Consistent Activity Ensembles and Phase Transitions
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jan Pyrzowski, Laura Messio, Guillaume Marrelec, Marcin Markiewicz
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a statistical-mechanical framework for spiking neuronal systems in which entire spike trains, defined as spatiotemporal configurations of discrete events, are treated as microstates of the system. Instead of modeling explicit network dynamics, we construct an ensemble over complete spike histories and assign to each configuration an effective energy functional that quantifies its consistency with intrinsic synaptic interactions. This formulation leads to a Boltzmann-like distribution over spike configurations, where an effective temperature captures the influence of external inputs acting as a stochastic drive. Macroscopic states are described in terms of coarse-grained observables, such as population firing-rate densities, and arise from a competition between energetic contributions favoring interaction-consistent spike patterns and entropic contributions favoring spatio-temporal disorder. Within this framework, we primarily characterize the transition between oscillatory and non-oscillatory activity. The non-oscillatory regime contains both broadly distributed, approximately uniform states and temporally localized collapsed states, whereas the oscillatory regime is characterized by repeated activity peaks. These regimes are diagnosed using order parameters derived from the population spike-rate density, including its entropy, temporal localization measures, and autocorrelation-based indicators. To complement the analytical treatment, we perform Monte Carlo simulations that sample the ensemble of admissible spike configurations using a Metropolis-Hastings scheme defined directly on spike trains. The simulations reveal the emergence of the predicted macroscopic regimes and provide a direct sampling-based probe of the free-energy landscape.

items.title: Neural Computation Runs on Dissipative Structures Under Cyclic Calibration: A Systems Perspective on Sleep
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Javier Diaz
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biological function operates far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustained by metastable structures that continuously cycle through synthesis, function execution, and degradation--consuming energy and exporting entropy in the process. Neural computation exemplifies this dissipative organization, relying on low-entropy structures engaged in dynamic processes that define key information transfer and processing parameters such as gain, threshold, and integration time. This perspective proposes that sleep serves as a systemic recalibration phase required to reset crucial signaling parameters that drift during dissipative processing. During wakefulness, neural activity progressively consumes and disrupts the organization of the very substrate from which it emerges, leading to parameter drift and reduced computational precision. Sleep maintains computational accuracy across activity cycles by recalibrating function-structure coupling--that is, by counterbalancing entropic drift. Rather than explaining the experimentally observed sleep need through homeostatic regulation of unknown physiological variables, this perspective reframes it as an emergent property of neural computation under thermodynamic constraints.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.21660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normative models chart how brain measures vary across the lifespan, expressing each individual as a deviation from a healthy reference. However, most regional models of cortical thickness disregard dependencies between cortical and subcortical anatomy, and transferring them to a new site typically requires retraining or a recalibration of location and scale alone. We condition lifespan norms of cortical thickness on subcortical volume, such that each deviation indicates whether an individual's cortex lies within the healthy range given their subcortical anatomy, and make them transferable. In 21,351 healthy individuals from 216 sites, conditioning on ten subcortical structures improved out-of-sample prediction on average, most for the amygdala and hippocampus. Refitting only the intercepts of all four distributional parameters on about 20 healthy individuals, as implemented in our open-source package NormGAMLSS, calibrated most of six unseen sites without retraining, for base and conditional models. In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, global deviation and structural dissociation (the reduction in mean absolute deviation under conditioning) predicted conversion to mild cognitive impairment and dementia beyond the Clinical Dementia Rating and dissociation added beyond global deviation for dementia, even at similar clinically recorded impairment. Conditional norms thus provide relevant, individual-level information.

items.title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shahryar G. Namdari, Francesco Iacomi, Riccardo Barbieri, Luca Mainardi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

items.title: How large an effect would we have seen? Positive controls, detection floors and dataset pitfalls in scalp-EEG speech decoding
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Blessing Isoyiza Adeika, Onyema Osuagwu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objective. Studies that decode imagined speech from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) commonly validate their pipelines with a positive control, usually overt speech, and report null results without stating what effect size the pipeline could have detected. Approach. Using ds003626 ("Thinking out loud"), KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, we audited decoding of overt speech, articulator preparation and imagined speech with artifact-channel subsets, band-limited decoding and trial selection, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion. We injected class-dependent effects of known amplitude into the real recordings to measure the detection floor of five decoder families, and we checked the ds003626 labels against the dataset's acquisition protocol. Main results. On ds003626, two lip electrodes decoded overt speech at 0.7430 and the eight external channels at 0.7068, against 0.4231 for the 128-channel scalp montage, and no decodable signal survived in the 8-30 Hz band. On the other two corpora, within-subject accuracy rose monotonically with frequency into the range dominated by muscle activity. Band-power logistic regression detected an injected 8-30 Hz desynchronization of 0.54 uV under a criterion fixed in advance, whereas a compact convolutional network (EEGNet) detected nothing within subject up to 4.31 uV. In ds003626, the condition codes are the reverse of the intuitive reading, the class encoding changed between public releases, and condition is a deterministic function of time within each session. Significance. In these corpora the overt-speech positive control is dominated by myogenic signal and cannot validate a decoding pipeline. We recommend that speech-decoding studies report band-limited and artifact-channel accuracy, the direction of accuracy across frequency, and a measured detection floor.

items.title: Two dissociable axes of brain hierarchical dynamics track universal and population-specific effects of mindfulness
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Victor Oswald, David Zarka, Riku Johannes Ihalainen, Gulshan Kumar, Rikkert Hindriks, Auretta Sonia Kummar, Helen Correia, Hakuei Fujiyama, Saketh Malipeddi, Ravindra P Nagendra, Arun Sasidharan, Bindu M Kutty, Steven Laureys, Prejaas K. B. Tewarie
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How mental training reshapes the temporal architecture of large-scale brain dynamics and how these mechanisms differ between healthy and clinically vulnerable populations remains poorly understood. Time-averaged neural measures collapse the multi-scale nature of brain activity, obscuring the dynamic processes through which behavioural interventions reorganise hierarchical brain function. Here, applying a sliding-window Temporal Irreversibility Index to source-reconstructed EEG across three complementary cohorts (n = 141), we decompose hierarchical brain trajectories into three orthogonal temporal descriptors and uncover two dissociable, mechanistically interpretable axes of intervention-induced plasticity. Cumulative meditation practice drives a universal, pan-cerebral reduction in the exploratory breadth of hierarchical dynamics, tracking dose-dependently with lifetime hours of practice. Temporal persistence is bidirectionally tuned by 8-week mindfulness-based interventions in a population-specific way: reduced in healthy meditators but increased in trauma-exposed individuals, revealing that comparable MBI protocols engage qualitatively distinct network mechanisms depending on baseline clinical status. A joint Hidden Markov Model further links these dynamical shifts to distinct microstate substrates, and longitudinal changes selectively track improvements in a single facet of mindfulness, attentional presence in daily life. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for how behavioural training reorganises non-equilibrium brain dynamics, with direct implications for tailoring mindfulness-based interventions to individual clinical profiles.

Here, applying a sliding-window Temporal Irreversibility Index to source-reconstructed EEG across three complementary cohorts (n = 141), we decompose hierarchical brain trajectories into three orthogonal temporal descriptors and uncover two dissociable, mechanistically interpretable axes of intervention-induced plasticity. Cumulative meditation practice drives a universal, pan-cerebral reduction in the exploratory breadth of hierarchical dynamics, tracking dose-dependently with lifetime hours of practice. Temporal persistence is bidirectionally tuned by 8-week mindfulness-based interventions in a population-specific way: reduced in healthy meditators but increased in trauma-exposed individuals, revealing that comparable MBI protocols engage qualitatively distinct network mechanisms depending on baseline clinical status. A joint Hidden Markov Model further links these dynamical shifts to distinct microstate substrates, and longitudinal changes selectively track improvements in a single facet of mindfulness, attentional presence in daily life. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for how behavioural training reorganises non-equilibrium brain dynamics, with direct implications for tailoring mindfulness-based interventions to individual clinical profiles.

items.title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Haruki Aoki, Kazufumi Tanji, Shohei Kiryu, Masahiro Takeoka, Junko Ishi-Hayase
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.

items.title: Limits of adaptive linear postprocessing in six-state quantum key distribution
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Toyohiro Tsurumaru
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-way classical communication improves the noise tolerance of quantum key distribution, but the limits of adaptive parity processing remain unclear. For the six-state protocol with equal three-basis error rate $p\in[p_*,1/2]$, where $p_*=(5-\sqrt5)/10\simeq27.64\%$, we construct a single compatible collective attack that defeats a broad class of linear postprocessing. Each public message may be an affine function of the sender's raw key, chosen adaptively from the public history. For every finite input length and every accepted transcript of positive probability, Eve's optimal probability of recovering any affine function of Alice's raw key is at least Bob's. Consequently, reliable agreement on a linear final key is incompatible with secrecy. The same conclusion holds for arbitrary publicly seeded privacy amplification after reliable recovery of a linear candidate. The proof conditions on the complete transcript, which restricts the two raw keys to affine subspaces. A local degradation of Eve's state, a known R\'enyi-entropy comparison, and a coset-probability inequality then give the recovery comparison. Both inequalities are proved in self-contained appendices. The result allows block splitting, regrouping, nonzero-syndrome selection, and adaptive linear reconciliation.

items.title: Finite-Frequency Boson-Number Bounds Across the Quantum Rabi Transition
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Razmik G. Unanyan, Michael Fleischhauer, Nikolay V. Vitanov
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the quantum Rabi model, a fundamental model of quantum optics describing a two-level system coupled to a bosonic mode, including counter-rotating terms. In the limit of large separation between the two-level transition frequency and the bosonic mode frequency, the model exhibits a quantum phase transition at a critical coupling strength. Although the model is exactly solvable, simple analytic expressions for important physical quantities are generally unavailable. We derive rigorous upper and lower bounds for the ground-state energy and boson occupation number across the quantum phase transition at finite frequency ratios. Our results characterize the subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes and establish the scaling behavior of the boson occupation near the critical point. Exact numerical diagonalization demonstrates the tightness of the derived bounds, while the resulting finite-frequency inequalities provide experimentally testable predictions for trapped-ion quantum simulators.

items.title: Reducing the Cost of Qudit State Preparation by Learning a Sparse Structure for SNAP Gates
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Marco Pennazio, Leonardo Ignazio Pagliochini, Riccardo Pellini, Maurizio Ferrari Dacrema, Paolo Cremonesi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing quantum states in bosonic qudits with SNAP--Displacement sequences requires both optimizing the gate parameters and deciding which Fock levels should be controlled by each SNAP gate. A fully parameterized ansatz assigns an independent phase to every Fock level in every gate, leading to a number of phases that grows steeply. This constitutes a problem for short to medium term systems as controlling many phases requires complex control pulses which are subject to increased control errors. Previous work reduced this cost by restricting the trainable phases to predefined sparse patterns, such as a diagonal or a grid, which however may not be optimal for a specific target state. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a method that learns which phases are needed together with their values, using a differentiable mask. A sparsity penalty encourages the removal of unnecessary phases, while temperature annealing gradually turns the masks into binary decisions. We compare the proposed method with fully parameterized and predefined sparse ansatzes on Fourier and Haar-random target states. The evaluation considers both the minimum number of phases required to reach different infidelity thresholds and the overall trade-off between fidelity and phases required, measured through Pareto frontiers and hypervolume. The results show that learning the location of the phases together with their values provides competitive or improved fidelity--resource trade-offs, although the advantage depends on the target state and qudit dimension.

items.title: Time-optimal robust quantum control for partially known errors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Lloren\c{c} Balada Gaggioli
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust quantum control usually assumes one of two extremes: the error is of a known form and only its strength is unknown, or nothing at all is known about it. In practice one often sits in between. The size of a static error is unknown, but its class is known, for example, it only shifts energy levels, or it acts on each subsystem separately. We ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class. A time-independent Hamiltonian can do this if and only if all errors in the class have zero diagonal in a common basis. In that case an equally spaced energy ladder in this basis does it after one period. A lower bound that holds for any time-dependent control with bounded drive power shows that this simple constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. Completely unknown errors need a time-dependent control, and there, knowing the error class shortens the minimum time by a factor $\sqrt{d^2+1}$. So partial knowledge of the error changes not only how long an optimal robust control takes, but also its form.

items.title: Practical Fidelity Estimation for Noisy Quantum Devices Using Direct and Survival-Probability-Based Protocols
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ahmed Aman, Kaustav Chatterjee, Younes Javanmard, Tanmoy Pandit
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable characterization of quantum states and quantum processes is central to the development of scalable quantum computing. Standard characterization techniques such as full quantum state tomography become rapidly impractical as system size increases. In this work we present two software-oriented fidelity estimation protocols that avoid full tomographic reconstruction while remaining experimentally relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The first protocol is direct fidelity estimation (DFE), where the fidelity between a target state and an experimentally prepared state is estimated from importance-sampled Pauli measurements. The second protocol is a survival-probability-based method that reconstructs fidelity from experimentally accessible moments of a noisy evolution and its approximate inverse, and is intrinsically robust against state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors. We discuss the theoretical basis of both approaches, analyze their noise sensitivity, and present numerical evidence on representative multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude-damping channels. For DFE we show that attenuation-aware correction improves robustness against measurement noise. For the survival-probability approach we show that an $L_2$-optimized expansion substantially outperforms naive Taylor truncation in high-noise regimes.

items.title: Driving the cooling process of a quantum system via classical noise
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: B. Militello, A. Napoli
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is known that under particular hypotheses anomalous thermalization processes can occur, such as the Mpemba effect, consisting in a faster cooling down when the system is prepared in a hotter initial condition, thus making convenient to warm up the system before the freezing process in order to make it freeze in a shorter time. It is shown here that the action of a Markovian classical noise during the freezing process can accelerate the approach to the zero-temperature thermal state. This prediction is counterintuitive, especially after observing that a classical noise can be considered equivalent to the action of an infinite-temperature reservoir, since both drive the system toward the same state. These facts lead to the statement that warming up the system during the contact with a low-temperature reservoir can accelerate the cooling process.

items.title: Quantum instanton approach to metastable collective spin systems: Numerical implementation and applications
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Maciej Chudak, Massimiliano Esposito, Krzysztof Ptaszynski
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven-dissipative collective spin systems can host several long-lived metastable states; rare switching between them governs slow relaxation and first-order dissipative phase transitions associated with changes in the dominant stationary state. In the companion Letter [arXiv:2604.15091], we introduced a quantum instanton framework based on exact quasiprobability dynamics to describe this switching and illustrated it with a minimal model possessing a simplifying symmetry. Here we develop its numerical implementation, combining collocation and shooting methods, and apply it to two microscopically motivated systems: the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model with purely collective dissipation and the cooperative resonance fluorescence with collective and local dissipation. By determining the leading exponential scaling of switching rates between metastable attractors, we predict the stationary magnetization, the first-order dissipative phase-transition point, and the exponential scaling of slow relaxation rates. These predictions agree with quantum master-equation calculations and an exact analytical result for the second model without dephasing. We also examine how the choice of quasiprobability representation affects numerical convergence and find that the alternative semiclassical Wigner approach, based on Gaussian truncation, has varying accuracy across models and parameter regimes. These results substantiate the framework's applicability to experimentally relevant collective spin systems with both collective and local dissipation.

items.title: Size-Dependent High-Order Harmonic Generation from Linear Carbon-Chain Molecules in Linearly Polarized Laser Fields
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yifan Kang, Yang Yang, Yingtan Li, Shuwen Pang, Huiwen Yang, Yingdan Zhang, Shushan Zhou
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-order harmonic generation from molecules is highly sensitive to molecular geometry and strong-field electron dynamics, providing a powerful route for probing and controlling ultrafast processes in extended systems. In this work, we systematically investigate the influence of molecular chain length on HHG from linear carbon-chain molecules C$_2$H$_2$, C$_6$H$_2$, and C$_{10}$H$_2$ driven by an 800 nm linearly polarized laser field. To isolate the molecular-size effect from the influence of different ionization potentials, the laser intensities are adjusted to maintain the same Keldysh parameter for different molecules. Real-time time-dependent density functional theory simulations are performed with the molecular axis aligned parallel to the laser polarization direction. The results show that increasing the molecular chain length significantly enhances the harmonic yield and tends to extend the cutoff region. In particular, C$_{10}$H$_2$ exhibits much stronger plateau harmonics than C$_2$H$_2$, while the intermediate molecule C$_6$H$_2$ shows harmonic intensities between those of C$_2$H$_2$ and C$_{10}$H$_2$. Time-frequency analysis and charge-density evolution reveal that the enhanced HHG emission in longer chains originates from the enlarged electron acceleration distance and increased probability of multi-center recollision, especially near the terminal carbon atoms. These findings demonstrate that molecular-size engineering offers an effective strategy for controlling harmonic emission and optimizing attosecond light sources in extended molecular systems.

items.title: Operator-Space Entanglement Entropy in Random Fermionic Gaussian Dynamics
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Pablo Bayona-Pena, Elena Gramellini, Lorenzo Piroli
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the von Neumann operator-space entanglement entropy (OSEE) of initial product operators evolved under random gaussian dynamics, as modeled by a Brownian SYK$_2$ model. By exploiting a mapping to a domain-wall melting problem, we derive an exact expression for the time-dependent bipartite OSEE in the thermodynamic limit, and obtain an analytic characterization of the corresponding gaussian Page curve emerging at late times. Our results build on recent work on the entanglement dynamics in the all-to-all quantum simple exclusion process, leveraging tools from RMT, including the Coulomb-gas approach and a mapping to the free Jacobi process. Finally, based on our results, we discuss the possibility of relating the OSEE with non-gaussianity measures in the Heisenberg picture.

items.title: Multiplicative Semidefinite Programming Upper Bounds on Quantum No-Signalling-Assisted Zero-Error Capacity
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xin Li, Yinan Li
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study zero-error communication and exact simulation of quantum channels assisted by quantum no-signalling correlations. For a channel with Kraus operator space $K$, we introduce a semidefinite programming parameter $\Gamma(K)$ that is exactly multiplicative under tensor products and upper-bounds $\Theta_{\rm NS}(K)$, where $\log_2\Theta_{\rm NS}(K)=C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ and $C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ denotes the asymptotic quantum no-signalling-assisted zero-error capacity. Among known upper bounds on $\Theta_{\rm NS}$ given by semidefinite programs, $\Gamma$ is the tightest. We also prove that the previously introduced simulation lower bound $\Sigma^{-}(K)$ is exactly multiplicative and satisfies $\Theta_{\rm NS}(K)\leq\Gamma(K)\leq\Sigma^{-}(K)\leq\Gamma(K)^2$. Using this multiplicativity, we show that neither $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\log_2\Sigma^{-}(K)$ nor its regularized extension $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\lim\nolimits_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log_2\Sigma^{-}(K^{\otimes n})$ holds in general. This answers an open question about the asymptotic simulation cost $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)$. For classical-quantum channels, we obtain sharp bounds. If $r$ is the effective output dimension, then $\Theta_{\rm NS}\leq\Gamma\leq(1+r^{1/2})\Theta_{\rm NS}/2$ and $\Gamma\leq\Sigma^{-}\leq(1+r^{1/2})\Gamma/2$. If $k$ is the minimum rank of the output support projections, then $\Sigma^{-}/\Theta_{\rm NS}\leq[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]^2$, and this bound is sharp for every $1\leq k\leq r$. Thus, we obtain the sharp bound $S_{0,\rm NS}-C_{0,\rm NS}\leq2\log_2[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]$.

items.title: Stitched surface codes: planar concatenation through GHZ corridors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Mohamed A. Shalby, Alexandre Bourassa, Amir Karamlou, Leigh Martin, Alexis Morvan, Nicholas Noll, Craig Gidney, Leonid P. Pryadko
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture that concatenates four distance-t rotated surface-code patches with the [[4,2,2]] outer code, encoding two logical qubits at code distance d = 2t in a physical footprint of N < 2(2t+1)^2 qubits on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity. The outer-code stabilizer generators XXXX and ZZZZ, each of physical weight 4t, are measured in situ via verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between adjacent patches, without lattice surgery or long-range gates. The outer-code gadgets introduce hyperedge fault mechanisms, but by design each decomposes into graphlike components, so the complete syndrome is decoded by a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass. Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates that scale as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Finally, we implement the construction experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in both the ZZ and XX memory bases. With the correlated-matching decoder, increasing the code distance from d = 4 to d = 6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52. The construction thus provides a near-term testbed for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Azadeh Alavi, Fatemeh Kouchmeshki, Hossein Akhoundi, Yongli Re, Abdolrahman Alavi, Muhammad Usman
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have reported promising results from quantum machine learning in drug discovery, healthcare, materials science and cybersecurity. Research includes comparisons with classical machine learning algorithms and the development of sequential hybrid pipelines. We propose that fusion can improve prediction when classical and quantum representations capture complementary predictive relationships. items.title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rahul Jain
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most \[ \exp[-\Omega(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \] for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+\delta$ is at most $\exp[-\Omega(\delta^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<\delta\le\varepsilon$. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

items.title: Optimising multipartite entanglement manipulation in quantum networks
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shashank Shekhar, David Elkouss, Siddhartha Santra
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-range, genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) between distant parties in a quantum network is a crucial resource for distributed quantum information processing. Through controlled manipulation of short-range GME states in the network via stochastic local operations aided by classical communication (SLOCC), long-range GME can be established between selected target nodes on demand. Optimizing such multipartite entanglement distribution protocols under constraints imposed by the network architecture, target-node set, and available resource budget is a key challenge in resource-efficient manipulation of GME. We present a general operational framework for manipulating GME in quantum networks by classifying the relevant networking operations into three broad primitives-inflation, deflation, and purification-reflecting their effect on the proliferation of GME through general bounds and illustrative examples. We show how these primitives can be combined to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, enabling their systematic optimization, and demonstrate the framework with a simple example. Applying our approach to networks of D\"ur-Cirac-Tarrach states reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes. More generally, our framework provides a systematic approach to the construction and optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols for scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.

items.title: Crossovers between Time-Bin and Energy-Time Entanglement in Homodyned Resonance Fluorescence
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zi-Qi Zeng, Jian Wang, Bang Wu, Zhiliang Yuan
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically investigate photonic entanglement generated by homodyning resonance fluorescence from a two-level emitter with a phase-locked laser field. Under weak excitation, increasing the relative laser-field amplitude produces crossovers from time-bin to energy--time and back to time-bin entanglement. The intermediate energy--time regime occurs near amplitude matching, where destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component, allowing the two-photon contributions to dominate the coincidence signal. We evaluate the resulting photon statistics and first-order coherence and characterize the entanglement through violations of the CHSH Bell inequality in a Franson interferometer. This scheme provides a route to controlling photonic entanglement through linear optics and coherent interference.

items.title: Accurate gap control of 3D-integrated superconducting quantum circuits using asymmetric indium architecture and multi-angle flip-chip bonding
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: L. Richard, N. Bruckmoser, J. Feigl, D. Bunch, A. Bhattacharjee, L. Koch, I. Tsitsilin, V. P. Bader, H. Hu, L. S\"odergren, S. Filipp
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flip-chip 3D integration is a key enabling technology for overcoming the routing and layout constraints of planar superconducting quantum processors, but it requires accurate and uniform control of the inter-chip spacing while preserving qubit coherence. In conventional processes, thick indium bumps are deposited symmetrically on both chips, while dedicated spacers are introduced to limit the residual tilt. Here, we present a flip-chip bonding process based on an asymmetric indium architecture, combining $20\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ thick indium bumps on the control chip with $200\,\mathrm{nm}$ thin indium pads on the qubit chip. Using electrical and microwave measurements, we demonstrate low resistance and low loss indium interconnects, and show that transmon qubits integrated with this process reach relaxation and coherence times of $T_1=(159\pm14)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $T_{\mathrm{2,echo}}=(294\pm42)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, respectively, comparable to planar devices. Combined with a multi angle compression procedure that suppresses systematic tilt, this approach reduces the average post bonding tilt to $(20\pm12)\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$. These results establish an asymmetric indium architecture combined with multi angle compression as a robust, coherence preserving route toward 3D integrated superconducting quantum processors.

items.title: Casimir forces on suspended thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Tze Ue Ngai, Zuocheng Zhang, Q. Zhang, Youssef Jeyar, Jingwei Li, Zhengtang Luo, Mauro Antezza, H. B. Chan
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the Casimir force on thin suspended dielectric layers covered with graphene, both theoretically and experimentally. Thermal effects of the Casimir force on graphene occur at separations significantly smaller compared to ordinary metals and dielectrics. At such small separations, the Casimir force is sufficiently strong to be measured experimentally. However, the presence of substrates to support the graphene significantly reduces the enhancement. We show theoretically that replacing the solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores this strong thermal dependence. One of the interacting objects is a solid gold plate. The other object is a suspended dielectric membrane made of either 15 nm of silicon oxide or 13 nm silicon nitride, covered with graphene. At a separation of $\sim$500 nm, theoretical predictions yield changes in the Casimir pressure of up to 54 % and 40 % for silicon oxide and silicon nitride, respectively, when the temperature is increased from 10 K to 294 K. Measurements were performed for graphene on a suspended silicon nitride membrane at room temperature, using a gold-coated sphere attached to a cantilever as the force sensor. The measured force gradient is consistent with the theoretical prediction, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, in part because of uncertainties in the optical properties of silicon nitride. Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane covered with graphene provides a substantial reduction of the Casimir force, which may facilitate the stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xuan Chen, Ruo-Yu Yin, Xiao-Wen Shang, Xi-Jun Yuan, Ze-Feng Lan, Hong-Jing Du, Yi-Jun Chang, Bao-Jing Liu, Wen-Hao Zhou, Xi Tan, Eli Barkai, Hao Tang, Xian-Min Jin
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. We show that the bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of both the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and the statistics of detection events. Using a three-dimensional photonic chip, we demonstrate on-demand state engineering through dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection, enabling the protection of topological corner states and excited-state shelving. We further observe the predicted transition of the total detection probability on an effectively infinite one-dimensional lattice and identify its microscopic origin in Floquet near-dark modes. These results establish periodic conditional measurements as a general framework for engineering conditional quantum states and manipulating event-detection statistics in monitored quantum dynamics.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Konstantin Antipin, Richik Sengupta
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact zero-energy eigenstates built from entangled dimers have recently been found in a large class of spin Hamiltonians. While the individual states have a simple structure, their superpositions can have very different entanglement properties. In this work, we study these superpositions for geometrically local spin-1/2 chains with periodic boundary conditions. Using stabilizer theory and polynomial methods, we characterize the subspace they span and find the minimum entanglement entropy between two halves of the chain. For Hamiltonians generated by a single local Pauli interaction with noncommuting translates, this minimum obeys a volume law at fixed interaction range. The structure of the least-entangled superpositions also suggests further exact eigenstate constructions, including zero-energy states separable between the two halves of the chain and states at nonzero energies.

items.title: Perfect and peak state transfer on IBM quantum hardware
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Priscilla Awuah, Krystal Guo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's $156$-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes $Q_2 = C_4$ and $Q_3$, and on the Hamming-weighted paths $\mathrm{HP}_n$, the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes $Q_n$, for $n$ up to $20$; peak state transfer on the $X_n$ family for $n$ up to $11$; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.

items.title: A tutorial on quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations of bimolecular collisions
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Karl P. Horn, Christiane P. Koch
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collisions between atoms and molecules govern how energy is exchanged and redistributed in the gas phase, underpinning phenomena from spectral line broadening and interstellar molecular excitation to the cooling and trapping of molecules. A quantitative account of these collisions requires connecting the theoretical description of the interaction between the collision partners to measurable quantities such as cross sections. However, scattering theory as presented in quantum mechanics textbooks does not readily translate into numerical methods. Here, we formulate the scattering problem in Dirac notation, as customary in present-day quantum mechanics courses, and show how to build a practical numerical framework from it. We derive the "coupled channel" representation of the scattering problem with correct asymptotic behaviour and introduce Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions, from which we calculate cross sections, the observables measured in scattering experiments. Starting from single channel scattering, we build up to the realistic collision of a ground-state atom with a diatomic molecule.

items.title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Nitin Jha, Prateek Paudel, Abhishek Parakh
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

items.title: Classification of quantum states through conserved operators
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Federico Petrovich, R. Rossignoli, M. Cerezo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted by a prescribed set of transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information. Here we develop a general classification framework based on conserved operators (COs), i.e., not necessarily hermitian matrices having the state of interest as an eigenstate. We first show that COs belonging to the algebra generating the allowed transformations can be obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix. Their number determines the dimension of the accessible orbit, while their algebraic structure and eigenvalues provide further constraints on state convertibility. We establish general bounds on the number of COs and prove that highest-weight states, like separable states in the case of $n$ qudits, attain the maximum. We also show how these operators generate parent Hamiltonians having the characterized state as an exact ground state. We then also consider positive zero-eigenvalue COs, which encode forbidden directions of reduced density matrices and incorporate rank-based constraints into the same framework. Applying this approach to multiqubit SLOCC, we obtain complementary classifications from algebraic and rank COs. While for $n\leq 3$ qubits both lead to the usual classes, for $n=4$ qubits they distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined. The combined classification yields 287 fixed types and $4$ continuous families for $n=5$ qubits, and 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families for $n=6$ qubits, providing, to our knowledge, the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data.

items.title: monoprop: Scaling Pauli and Majorana propagation via Anticommutation Indices
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Aaron Miller
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce monoprop, an open-source, massively parallel operator-propagation framework for fermion and qubit bases. For $N$ qubits or modes, existing codes represent each of the $K$ tracked operator terms (Pauli strings or products of Majorana operators) as a $2N$-bit string, testing each for anticommutation with the gate at $O(KN)$ cost per gate. Here, we introduce the anticommutation index which rapidly looks up the terms anticommuting with a gate. A local gate changes only the terms that touch its sites, and when terms are truncated to act on few sites, only a fraction $\sim1/N$ touch any given qubit or mode, and we use this to prove the time per gate scales as $O(K/N)$. This counterintuitive result tells us that for a fixed number of terms, increasing the number of sites can make things faster. We demonstrate this numerically, and show monoprop scales almost ideally to 8192 cores, tracking $9.5\times10^{10}$ terms. Beyond propagation, we present memory-efficient surrogate graphs, which record one propagation and replay it at new angles, for fast energy re-estimation and parameter gradients, and an efficient method for finding energy-minimising gates and optimal angles for simulating adaptive quantum-chemistry circuits.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Silvie Ill\'esov\'a, Vojt\v{e}ch Nov\'ak, Martin Beseda
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drone-delivery planning combines routing decisions with operational constraints such as payload capacity and limited onboard energy, resulting in combinatorial optimization problems that can become costly to encode directly in binary form. This work investigates a hybrid quantum--classical approach in which candidate drone missions are generated and evaluated classically before constructing a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model for mission selection. Payload- and energy-infeasible missions are removed during preprocessing, while the reduced QUBO is solved using exact enumeration, simulated annealing (SA), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) used as a classical reference. Experiments on controlled synthetic delivery instances evaluate solution quality, the effect of preprocessing, and computational scaling. Exact QUBO optimization reproduces the MILP optimum on the evaluated small instances, while SA achieves $100\%$ feasibility with a median optimality gap of $0\%$. items.title: Singular wave functions and quantum collapse in inverse-power potentials
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hidetsugu Sakaguchi, Boris Malomed
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum collapse (QC) occurs under the action of the inverse-power potential U(r)=-U_{0}/(2r^{n}) in the framework of the Schroedinger equation. The corresponding stationary wave functions feature an infinite number of spatial oscillations at $r\rightarrow 0$. The ground state (GS) is missing in the presence of the QC, but the available bound states at finite energies may be physically relevant, as they are normalizable. This work aims to produce singular stationary wave functions. The analytical findings represent an asymptotic form of the stationary wave functions at $r\rightarrow 0$, which fill a continuous spectrum, and some exact solutions for the wave functions, obtained under appropriate conditions. As a regularized version, we also consider the potential truncated at a finite difference from the center. The regularized wave functions feature a finite number of spatial oscillations, the missing GS reappears, and the spectrum of the bound states is discrete.

items.title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shi-Yao Hou, Zipeng Wu, Chao Zhang, Guanru Feng, Keren Li, Jingen Xiang
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

items.title: Alternating Squeezing and Photon Subtraction for Optical Cat-State Generation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Johanna Conrad, Fabian Steinlechner, Ren\'{e} Sondenheimer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Schr\"{o}dinger cat states are important non-Gaussian resources for quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced metrology. Although photon subtraction from squeezed vacuum states has proven useful for generating such states in the optical domain, scaling to large amplitudes while maintaining high fidelity and heralding probability remains challenging. To address these obstacles, we analyze alternating squeezing and photon-number-subtraction operations. Rather than optimizing for a single heralding outcome, we formulate cat-state generation as a fidelity-constrained multibranch problem, jointly optimizing the total probability of all photon-number outcomes satisfying a prescribed fidelity threshold at one common experimental setting. Already for plain photon subtraction, this provides a more operational measure of the usable generation probability and can favor parameter configurations that differ from single-branch optima. Considering experimental constraints on available squeezing and photon-number-resolving capability, we demonstrate improvements in fidelity and success probability compared with plain photon subtraction, without necessarily increasing the required squeezing resources. Without restrictions on photon-number resolution, we find that the optimal architecture of the alternating scheme reduces to one of two single-subtraction endpoint configurations, depending on the available squeezing resources. When photon-number resolution is additionally limited, genuinely alternating branches can become advantageous. We derive analytical expressions for the conditional states, cat-state fidelities, and heralding probabilities, enabling efficient multibranch optimization and a systematic analysis of resource trade-offs, sensitivity to experimental parameter deviations, and heralding loss. Together, these results identify the architecture best suited to a given resource budget.

items.title: A constructive solution to the $n$-representability problem
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Nicholas C. Rubin, A. Eugene DePrince III
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a solution to the fermionic quantum marginal problem by constructing the complete family of two-body witnesses at each level of a weighted sum-of-squares hierarchy. Our construction combines positive-semidefinite Gram matrices with explicit linear nullspace constraints that exactly cancel all higher-body contributions, replacing the search for individual representability conditions with a systematic algebraic procedure. Beyond the completeness proof, we demonstrate the construction numerically by solving the associated semidefinite program and recovering the exact ground-state energy of a Richardson Hamiltonian in the three-fermion sector. We further prove that higher-degree particle-number multipliers are unnecessary when the full sum-of-squares generating algebra is used. These results establish a unified constructive framework for verifying the physicality of a candidate two-particle reduced density matrix through a complete characterization of all two-body witnesses.

items.title: Standard and Bipolar Rectification in Tilted Periodically-Driven Quantum Systems
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Joaqu\'in Pe\~{n}uela-Parra, Juan Jos\'e Mendoza-Arenas
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing mechanisms to control transport in correlated quantum systems is essential for advancing quantum circuit technologies. In this work, we establish a rectification mechanism for both particle and energy flow in a fermionic system coupled to external baths, in the presence of a tilted potential modulated locally by a time-periodic drive. The drive generates particle and energy currents even in the absence of chemical or thermal bias between the baths. These drive-induced currents are enhanced at resonant frequencies at which avoided crossings occur in the Floquet quasienergy spectrum, reflecting the role of the Floquet states as intermediate channels for transport. Once a bias between the baths is introduced, the drive-induced current contribution can reinforce, compete with, or even cancel the bias-induced contribution. These effects enable rectification in the non-interacting regime, which we quantify via the rectification coefficient $\mathcal{R}$. This coefficient measures the asymmetry between transport up the tilt (forward bias) and down the tilt (reverse bias). In addition to standard rectification, where transport is reduced under reverse bias, we identify a regime of bipolar rectification, in which the current flows only up the tilt regardless of the bias polarity. At the boundary between standard and bipolar regimes, the system achieves perfect rectification, corresponding to complete suppression of the reverse-bias current. In the presence of interactions between particles, the parameter region that supports bipolar rectification is enlarged and $\mathcal{R}$ can be enhanced by many orders of magnitude. Our results establish a rectification mechanism for particle and energy transport that can be experimentally realized in condensed matter and cold atom systems.

items.title: The Lov\'asz number is not alone: a continuum of R\'enyi points in the entanglement-assisted spectrum of graphs
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Nidhal Mghirbi, Seth Douglas
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Li and Zuiddam's entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum of graphs consists of the normalized graph parameters that are additive under disjoint unions, multiplicative under strong products and monotone under entanglement-assisted cohomomorphisms; the entanglement-assisted Shannon capacity is their pointwise minimum. To our knowledge, the Lov\'asz number $\vartheta$ was its only known element. We find a continuum of others. Three quantities of Duan and Winter, $\log_2\vartheta$, the minimal Holevo capacity $C_{\min}$ and the logarithm of the no-signalling simulation cost $\Sigma$, are the smallest information radii of classical-quantum channels compatible with a graph, measured with Petz-R\'enyi divergences of orders $0$, $1$ and $2$. At order zero this is due to Schrijver (as credited by Dalai) and to Duan and Winter; at order one it is the min-max formula for the Holevo capacity. Interpolating in the order gives a family $\vartheta_\alpha$, $0\le\alpha\le2$, and we prove that every member lies in the spectrum. The main step, multiplicativity under strong products for channels that need not factor, follows from an exact nesting identity for compressions. Sandwiched R\'enyi radii of order $\beta\in[1/2,\infty]$ give the same family, at $\alpha=2-1/\beta$. On the five-cycle the family takes every value in $[\sqrt5,5/2]$. A Hilbert-Schmidt inequality for the pentagon gives $C_{\min}(C_5)=\log_2(5/2)$, proving a conjecture of Duan and Winter. We also settle the two open links of their inequality chain: the graph-level no-signalling simulation rate always equals its single-letter value $\log_2\Sigma(G)$, and a 32-vertex graph from the Mermin-Peres magic square has $C_{\min}<\log_2\Sigma$, certified in exact rational arithmetic. Finally, $\Sigma$ never exceeds the projective rank of the complement; a rank inequality for the same square makes this strict on a 1440-vertex graph.

items.title: Infinite magic and the emergence of the continuum
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Leo Shaposhnik, Lorenzo Leone, Lennart Bittel, Dimitris Saraidaris, Alexander Jahn, Jens Eisert
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which features of a quantum state are needed for a relativistic quantum field theory to emerge from a lattice system? We address this question by establishing a quantitative relationship between the type classification of hyperfinite von Neumann algebras and the quantum-information-theoretic resource of nonstabilizerness, also called magic. Our results establish two complementary parts of this relationship. First, we prove that any stabilizer system on a lattice defines a canonical GNS Hilbert space in which local von Neumann algebras do not contain type III factors in their central decomposition. As an explicit example, we prove that for stabilizer systems with short-range order, the local algebras are isomorphic to tensor products of hyperfinite factors of type I or type II. This demonstrates that the absence of magic is accompanied by the absence of type III factors in the local algebras, therefore prohibiting the appearance of a quantum field theory. Second, for the hyperfinite factors of Araki, Woods and Powers, we prove a quantitative equivalence: The limiting factor is of type III if and only if the locally optimized min-relative entropy of magic diverges. This divergence is necessary to generate the continuous spectrum associated to a type III factor. Thus, in this setting, the emergence of a type III factor requires not merely the presence of magic, but an infinite amount of it. These results provide a rigorous setting supporting the proposal that infinite magic is a necessary structural ingredient for the emergence of a relativistic continuum from lattice systems.

items.title: Sparse-QITE: Discovering Compact Generators for Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution via Regularization Methods
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rafael G\'omez-Lurbe, Luca Ion, Alberto Acevedo, Andreu Angl\'es-Castillo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) provides a systematic route to ground-state preparation, but its cost grows rapidly with the locality $D$ of the unitary approximation, for which the local Pauli basis scales as $4^D$. We introduce Sparse-QITE, a regularized formulation that promotes compact generators, reducing the number of quantum operations and yielding circuits with fewer gates and lower depth. We derive rigorous bounds on the sparsification error and benchmark the method in one-dimensional transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models. Sparse-QITE exhibits a controllable sparsity--accuracy trade-off while retaining strong compression even in the high-accuracy regime. In scalability experiments with respect to $D$, the active support grows much more slowly than in standard QITE and, in several regimes, approximately saturates over the domain sizes studied. After circuit construction and transpilation, some of the largest-domain cases require only about $1\%$ of the standard-QITE gate count while maintaining high accuracy. We further introduce adaptive and active-discovery variants: the former selects the regularization strength dynamically during the evolution, while the latter reduces the number of Pauli expectation values that need to be evaluated and, consequently, the measurement requirements. These results establish sparsity-promoting regularization as a route toward more resource-efficient QITE. More broadly, these results suggest that sparsity-promoting regularization may also benefit variational quantum algorithms.

items.title: Syndrome-Resolved Decoding of Qubit Readout Errors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Han Zheng, Vladimir Pe\v{s}i\'c, Nikolay Gusarov, Andrea Lizzit, Taketo Imaizumi, Chulwoo Ahn, Marco Nicolas Mueller, Raymond Mencia, Edoardo Charbon, Vladimir E. Manucharyan
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readout errors in superconducting qubits include incorrect state assignment, bit flips within the computational subspace, and leakage to non-computational states. These errors require different mitigation strategies, yet conventional measurement fidelity and repeatability metrics do not resolve their individual contributions. Previous repeated-readout studies have shown that temporal correlations reveal additional information about readout errors. Here we introduce the Readout Error Decoder (RED), which converts repeated thresholded binary records into a channel-resolved error budget. Controlled error injections validate the channel-specific response of the decoder. We demonstrate RED on both fluxonium and transmon qubits and across distinct leakage-lifetime regimes. RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, providing a basis for targeted readout optimization across different qubit modalities.

items.title: Mechanical trisqueezing in circuit quantum acoustodynamics with SNAIL devices
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yi-Zhou Bu, Matteo Fadel, Kai Xu, Heng Fan
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum information processing with mechanical oscillators requires a uni- versal gate set, including a genuine non-Gaussian evolution. While circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) experiments have realized bilinear and quartic (four-wave mixing) operations by coupling mechanical modes to transmon qubits, the intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity of these devices precludes access to odd-order effective Hamiltonians such as trisqueezing. Here we propose a cQAD architec- ture in which a mechanical mode, hosted in a high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonator (HBAR), is coupled to a superconducting nonlinear asymmetric inductive element (SNAIL). By combining the cubic nonlinearity of the SNAIL with parametric flux driving, we engineer a three-wave mixing interaction that generates trisqueezed mechanical states, producing the characteristic triangular, star-shaped Wigner function with negative regions indicative of non-Gaussianity. We derive the effective trisqueezing Hamiltonian from the full circuit model, identify the drive frequencies and flux modulation required to isolate the desired interaction from competing terms, and quantify the achievable coupling strengths for parameters compatible with current fabrication capabilities. Our results establish a hardware-efficient route to non-Gaussian resource generation in mechanical quantum systems, extending the toolbox of cQAD toward universal continuous-variable quantum computation and enhanced quantum-limited sensing.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Alexander Nico-Katz
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The partial information decomposition (PID) framework is an extension of classical information theory that enables a systematic analysis of the structure of information in multipartite systems. We advance a simple extension of this framework enabling the construction of multipartite quantum PIDs (QPIDs); generalizing recent, exclusively bipartite, extensions. We construct two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity. First a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information. Second a sophisticated QPID enabled by our development of an operational partial order on quantum ensembles in terms of ensemble (inter-)convertability. Finally, as a concrete example of how QPIDs can be applied, we investigate objectivity scenarios; using our Holevo QPIDs to directly quantify objective information in extended graph states. These findings ultimately establish a foundation upon which generic multipartite QPIDs can be systematically constructed, introduce an operational partial order on ensembles, advance QPIDs as interesting objects of study in their own right, and demonstrate their immediate applicability to problems in quantum information.
